The oscillating magnet induces an alternating current, and **Lenz's law** damps the
oscillation so the swings die away.
**Step 1 — see why there is a deflection at all.** As the magnet moves in and out of the
coil, the flux through the coil **changes**, inducing an emf ✓ The galvanometer
registers the resulting current.
**Step 2 — see why it deflects both ways.** On the way **in** the flux increases; on the
way **out** it decreases ✓ The induced current reverses with each half-oscillation, so
the needle swings **left and right** alternately.
**Step 3 — see why the amplitude falls.** By Lenz's law the induced current always
**opposes the motion** that creates it ✓ The coil therefore exerts a retarding force on
the magnet throughout - repelling it as it approaches and attracting it as it recedes -
and the oscillation is **damped**.
**Step 4 — conclude.** The galvanometer deflects to **left and right**, with the
amplitude **steadily decreasing** ✓
**Where the energy goes.** The magnet's mechanical energy is converted into
**electrical** energy in the coil and then dissipated as **heat** in its resistance ✓
This is **electromagnetic damping**, and it is why the magnet eventually comes to rest
far sooner than friction alone would bring it.
**The energy argument against the alternative.** If the oscillation continued
undiminished while a current flowed, energy would be created from nothing ✓ The
damping is not incidental - it is required by conservation of energy.
**Why the deflection is not one-sided.** A one-sided deflection would need the flux to
change always in the same sense ✓ Here it alternates, so the current must alternate too.
**The same effect elsewhere.** A magnet dropped down a copper pipe falls remarkably
slowly, for exactly this reason ✓ The induced eddy currents oppose its motion at every
stage.
**What would change the behaviour.** Opening the circuit stops the current, and with it
the damping ✓ The magnet then oscillates almost freely - a striking demonstration that
it is the **current**, not the magnetic field as such, that does the braking.
∴ G shows deflection to the left and right but the amplitude steadily decreases.

Apply F̄ = qv̄ x B̄, remembering that the electron's charge is **negative**.
**Step 1 — set up directions.** Take east as **+x**, north as **+y** and up as **+z**.
The electrons move **south to north**, so
v̄ = v **ŷ** ✓
The vertical component of the Earth's field points **down**, so
B̄ = −B **ẑ** ✓
**Step 2 — evaluate the cross product.**
v̄ x B̄ = (v ŷ) x (−B ẑ)
= −vB (ŷ x ẑ)
= **−vB x̂** - pointing **west** ✓
**Step 3 — apply the negative charge.** For an electron q = −e, so
F̄ = (−e)(−vB x̂)
= **+evB x̂** - pointing **east** ✓
**Step 4 — conclude.** The beam is deflected **towards the east** ✓
**Why the sign of the charge matters so much.** A positive charge moving the same way
would be pushed **west** ✓ Half the difficulty in such problems is remembering that the
electron reverses the direction given by v̄ x B̄.
**A quicker route with the left hand.** For an **electron**, take the conventional
current as flowing **opposite** to the motion - that is, north to south ✓ Fleming's
left-hand rule with the first finger down (field), second finger south (current), gives
the thumb pointing **east** ✓ the same answer.
**Why only the vertical component matters.** The horizontal component of the Earth's
field points **north**, parallel to the electron's velocity ✓ and v̄ x B̄ vanishes for
parallel vectors, so it contributes no force at all.
**Why this mattered in practice.** Old television tubes had to be adjusted for the
Earth's field, which varies with latitude ✓ A set shipped from one hemisphere to another
needed its picture re-centred - and large tubes carried a mu-metal shield for exactly
this reason.
**Reading the distractors.** **West** ✗ is the direction for a positive charge. **No
deflection** ✗ would need v̄ parallel to B̄. **North to south** ✗ is along the velocity,
but a magnetic force is always **perpendicular** to it ✓
∴ East.

Maxwell's equations give the speed of light as **1/√(µ₀ε₀)**.
**Step 1 — state the result.**
**c = 1/√(µ₀ε₀) = √[1/(µ₀ε₀)]** ✓
**Step 2 — verify it numerically.**
µ₀ = 4π x 10⁻⁷ = **1·2566 x 10⁻⁶** T m A⁻¹
ε₀ = **8·854 x 10⁻¹²** C² N⁻¹ m⁻²
µ₀ε₀ = **1·1127 x 10⁻¹⁷**
√(µ₀ε₀) = 3·336 x 10⁻⁹
c = 1/3·336 x 10⁻⁹ = **3·00 x 10⁸ m s⁻¹** ✓
**Why this was so important.** Maxwell computed the combination from measurements of
**electrical** and **magnetic** constants made in the laboratory, with no reference to
light at all ✓ The answer matched the measured speed of light exactly, and he concluded
that light **is** an electromagnetic wave - one of the great unifications in physics.
**Checking the dimensions.**
[µ₀ε₀] = [T m A⁻¹][C² N⁻¹ m⁻²]
works out to **s² m⁻²** ✓
so 1/√(µ₀ε₀) has units of **m s⁻¹**, a speed ✓ The option √(µ₀ε₀) would be the
reciprocal of a speed, and the two ratio forms have no sensible units at all.
**The analogy with mechanical waves.** For a wave on a string, v = √(T/µ) - the
restoring agency over the inertial one ✓ For light, 1/ε₀ plays the part of the
"stiffness" of space and µ₀ that of its "inertia".
**What happens in a medium.**
v = 1/√(µε) = c/√(µ_r ε_r) = **c/n** ✓
so the refractive index is n = √(µ_r ε_r) - the same relation that links optics to
electromagnetism.
**The modern status of c.** Since 1983 the metre has been **defined** from c, which is
now fixed at exactly **299 792 458 m s⁻¹** ✓ and in 2019 µ₀ ceased to be exact, being
determined instead by measurement.
**Reading the distractors.** **√(µ₀ε₀)** ✗ is 1/c, about 3·3 x 10⁻⁹ s m⁻¹. The two
**ratios** ✗ have neither the right value nor the right dimensions ✓
∴ √[1/(µ₀ε₀)].

A susceptibility of 400 - large and positive - is the signature of a **ferromagnet**.
**Step 1 — recall the ranges.**
**diamagnetic**: χ small and **negative**, about −10⁻⁵ ✓
**paramagnetic**: χ small and **positive**, about +10⁻⁵ to 10⁻³ ✓
**ferromagnetic**: χ **very large** and positive, from hundreds to hundreds of
thousands ✓
**Step 2 — place the value.** χ = **400** is positive and enormous compared with any
paramagnet, so the material is **ferromagnetic** ✓
**Why ferromagnets have such huge susceptibilities.** Neighbouring atomic moments are
locked parallel by the **exchange interaction**, forming **domains** ✓ A modest applied
field only has to grow the favourably aligned domains, not fight thermal disorder
atom by atom - so the magnetisation produced is vast.
**Typical values, for comparison.**
bismuth: χ = **−1·7 x 10⁻⁴** (diamagnetic)
aluminium: χ = **+2·2 x 10⁻⁵** (paramagnetic)
iron: χ up to **10⁵** (ferromagnetic) ✓
**The three defining tests.**
**sign**: negative means diamagnetic ✓
**magnitude**: much greater than 1 means ferromagnetic ✓
**temperature dependence**: paramagnets follow χ = C/T; ferromagnets lose their
ferromagnetism above the Curie point ✓
**What the relative permeability would be.**
µ_r = 1 + χ = **401** ✓ so the material concentrates flux four hundredfold - which is
exactly why transformer and motor cores are made of iron.
**Why "ferroelectric" is not a magnetic class at all.** It describes a material with
spontaneous **electric** polarisation, such as barium titanate ✓ The word is the
electrical analogue of ferromagnetic and has nothing to do with magnetic
susceptibility - a trap for the hurried reader.
**Reading the other distractors.** **Diamagnetic** ✗ requires a negative χ.
**Paramagnetic** ✗ requires χ of order 10⁻⁵, some seven orders of magnitude smaller ✓
∴ Ferromagnetic.

Curie's law makes the susceptibility of a paramagnet **inversely proportional** to the
absolute temperature.
**Step 1 — state the law.**
χ = C/T ✓ with T in **kelvin**.
**Step 2 — convert both temperatures.**
−73 °C = 273 − 73 = **200 K**
−173 °C = 273 − 173 = **100 K** ✓
**Step 3 — form the ratio.**
χ₂/χ₁ = T₁/T₂
= 200/100
= **2**
**Step 4 — compute.**
χ₂ = 2 x 0·0075
= **0·015** ✓
**Why cooling raises the susceptibility.** Paramagnetism is a contest between the
aligning influence of the applied field and the **randomising** effect of thermal
motion ✓ Cooling weakens the randomisation, so a given field aligns more of the moments
and the material magnetises more readily.
**Why kelvin and not celsius.** The law is χ ∝ 1/T with T the **absolute**
temperature ✓ Using −73 and −173 directly would give a ratio of 173/73 = 2·37 and a
negative susceptibility along the way - both nonsense. Converting to kelvin is the
essential first step.
**The Curie constant here.**
C = χT = 0·0075 x 200 = **1·5 K** ✓
and a check: at 100 K, χ = 1·5/100 = **0·015** ✓
**What happens as T approaches zero.** χ grows without limit ✓ In practice the law
fails at very low temperatures, where the moments begin to interact and the material
may order magnetically - and χ saturates, since the magnetisation cannot exceed full
alignment.
**The ferromagnetic version.** Above the Curie point, χ = C/(T − T_C) ✓ the Curie-Weiss
law, with the same 1/T character but shifted.
**Reading the distractors.** **0·0075** ✗ assumes no change with temperature. **0·0045**
✗ and **0·0030** ✗ would correspond to **higher** temperatures (333 K and 500 K), but
the material has been **cooled** ✓ The susceptibility must rise, which rules out both at
a glance.
∴ 0.015.

A conductor flying through the Earth's field develops a motional emf **Blv**, using the
component of B perpendicular to the plane swept out.
**Step 1 — convert the speed.**
1080 km/h = 1080 x (1000/3600)
= **300 m s⁻¹** ✓
**Step 2 — identify the relevant field component.** The wings are horizontal and the
aircraft flies horizontally, so the area swept by the wingspan is **horizontal** ✓ Only
the **vertical** component of the Earth's field threads it - which is the 1·75 x 10⁻⁵ T
given.
**Step 3 — apply the motional emf formula.**
e = B_v l v
= (1·75 x 10⁻⁵)(40)(300)
**Step 4 — evaluate.**
1·75 x 10⁻⁵ x 40 = **7 x 10⁻⁴**
7 x 10⁻⁴ x 300 = **0·21 V** ✓
**Where the emf comes from.** Each free electron in the wing moves with the aircraft and
feels a force qv̄ x B̄ **along** the wing ✓ Charge accumulates at one wingtip until the
electrostatic field it creates balances the magnetic force - and the resulting potential
difference is the emf.
**Which wingtip is positive.** With the aircraft flying **east** and the vertical field
pointing **down** (northern hemisphere), the force on a positive charge is
v̄ x B̄ = east x down = **south** ✓ so the southern - here the right-hand - wingtip
becomes positive.
**Why the horizontal component is ignored.** It is parallel to the horizontal area swept
and threads **no** flux through it ✓ It would matter for an aircraft climbing or
diving.
**Can this emf be used?** No ✓ There is no circuit: the air is an insulator, so no
current flows and no energy is extracted. The 0·21 V exists but can do nothing - though
it is measurable between the wingtips with a sensitive voltmeter carried on board.
**A sense of the scale.** 0·21 V is about a seventh of a torch battery ✓ small, but
easily detectable, and the effect is exploited in **electromagnetic flow meters**, where
a conducting fluid replaces the aircraft.
**Reading the distractors.** **2·1 V** ✗ is ten times too large, from a slip in the
powers of ten. **0·5 V** ✗ and **0·34 V** ✗ match no product of the given numbers ✓
∴ 0.21 V.

Three of the four statements are true of every bar magnet; the fourth denies what a
magnet is.
**Step 1 — test "it doesn't produce a magnetic field".** This is plainly **false** ✓
Producing a magnetic field is the defining property of a magnet. Iron filings sprinkled
near it map the field at once, and a compass needle responds to it.
**Step 2 — check the other three.**
"**its poles cannot be separated**" ✓ **true** - break a bar magnet in two and each
piece is a complete magnet with its own north and south pole. No **magnetic monopole**
has ever been found, and
∇·B̄ = 0 ✓ expresses that fact.
"**it points north-south when suspended**" ✓ **true** - freely suspended, it aligns with
the Earth's magnetic field, which is the basis of the compass.
"**like poles repel, unlike attract**" ✓ **true** - the magnetic analogue of Coulomb's
rule for charges.
**Step 3 — conclude.** The **false** statement is that a bar magnet produces no
magnetic field ✓
**Why poles cannot be separated.** Magnetism arises from **circulating currents** -
ultimately from electron spin and orbital motion ✓ Every current loop is inherently a
**dipole**, with two poles, so no isolated pole can exist. This is the deepest contrast
between magnetism and electrostatics, where isolated charges are commonplace.
**The field a bar magnet makes.** Lines emerge from the **north** pole, curve round
through space and re-enter at the **south**, continuing **inside** the magnet from south
to north ✓ They form **closed loops**, unlike electrostatic field lines, which begin and
end on charges.
**Why the north pole points north.** The Earth's geographic north is a magnetic
**south** pole ✓ which is why the north-seeking end of a compass is attracted to it - a
piece of terminology that has confused students since Gilbert.
**The dipole moment.** m = pole strength x length, measured in A m² ✓ It is what
determines the torque m̄ x B̄ the magnet feels in an external field.
∴ it doesn't produce magnetic field.

A ferromagnet magnetises enormously easily, so its susceptibility is **much greater than
1**.
**Step 1 — recall the definition.**
χ = M/H ✓
the magnetisation produced per unit applied field strength.
**Step 2 — place the three classes.**
**diamagnetic**: χ small and **negative**, about −10⁻⁵ - the material weakly opposes the
field
**paramagnetic**: χ small and **positive**, about 10⁻⁵ to 10⁻³
**ferromagnetic**: χ **≫ 1**, from hundreds to hundreds of thousands ✓
**Step 3 — conclude.** For a ferromagnetic substance, **χ ≫ 1** ✓
**Typical values.**
soft iron: χ up to **5000**
mu-metal: up to **10⁵** ✓
permalloy, used in transformer cores, similar
**Why ferromagnets are so different in degree.** The **exchange interaction** aligns
neighbouring atomic moments spontaneously into **domains**, each already fully
magnetised ✓ An applied field need only grow the favourably oriented domains and rotate
the rest - a far easier task than aligning individual atoms against thermal motion, as
in a paramagnet.
**A caution about the value.** For a ferromagnet χ is **not a constant** ✓ It depends on
the applied field and on the sample's magnetic history, because of **hysteresis**.
Quoting a single number, as the question does, means an approximate initial
susceptibility.
**The related quantity.**
µ_r = 1 + χ ✓
so a ferromagnet with χ = 5000 has µ_r ≈ 5001 - which is why an iron core multiplies a
coil's inductance thousands of times.
**What happens above the Curie point.** The exchange ordering collapses and the material
becomes an ordinary paramagnet with χ of order 10⁻³ ✓ For iron that happens at 1043 K.
**Reading the distractors.** **χ > 1** ✗ is true but far too weak a statement - it would
also admit a material with χ = 1·5, which is not ferromagnetic. **χ < 1** ✗ describes
para- and diamagnets. **Zero** ✗ describes a vacuum ✓ The question asks what
characterises ferromagnetism, and only "much greater than 1" does.
∴ ≫ 1.
